newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA NEEDS NEW LAW TO FIGHT ORGANISED CRIME.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA NEEDS NEW LAW TO FIGHT ORGANISED CRIME.

text.p: Bulgaria's interior ministry said on Tuesday current legislation did not provide enough powers to combat street and organised crime, which appeared to be much worse than the former Socialist rulers had admitted.
Slavcho Bosilkov, head of the ministry's National Police Directorate, told a news conference that official crime figures had been falsified under the previous government.

"In the first two months of this year 31,924 crimes were committed, which is some 7,000 up from the same period in 1996, but I think that last year's figures were intentionally reduced under certain instructions," he said.
He did not elaborate on who had given the instructions but said it appeared to be a long standing practice which dated back to one-party rule before 1989.

The ex-communist Socialist government was toppled last month after 30 days of street protests. The interim cabinet sacked ministry department heads as part of a general clean-up of state institutions.
Bosilkov said that Bulgaria urgently needed to update its legislation in order to combat rising street and organised crime.

Under current criminal justice laws, video tapes, diskettes and other information media cannot be admitted as evidence in court cases, which Bosilkov said was a "serious obstacle for cracking down on organised criminal groups".

"We were aware of the names of perpetrators of some of the country's most outrageous killings but gaps in the legislation did not allowed us to take them and their criminal group to the prosecution and the court," he said.

Bulgaria's crime rate has soared since the collapse of communist rule in 1989. Mafia-style killings have caused a public outcry but the poorly-paid police are ill-equipped to act and vulnerable to corruption.
Former Prime Minister Andrei Lukanov was shot dead in front of his home last October but perpetrators are still unknown.
